question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
## Short answer
**The retrieved documents don't cover 1 November 2019, so I can't tell you what the law said on that date.** The earliest version I found is dated 7 September 2022. I haven't filled the gap from memory. Everything below comes from later versions, so treat it as a guide to what to check and confirm it against the 2019 version of the Act.

## What the law says (later versions only)
- **Retaliation protection (Residential Tenancies Act 1997, file "rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf", 7 Sept 2022, v101 per the file name).** Some notices to vacate have no effect if they were given in response to the renter exercising, or proposing to exercise, a right under the Act. The same applies if they were given in response to the renter making a report under section 72AA [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). In that version, this protection is stated for notices under sections 91ZZD, 91ZZDA, 91ZZEA and 91ZZEB [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). I can't tell from these excerpts whether it reaches a notice to a month-to-month renter like you, or what a 2019 notice would have been called.
- **Reporting damage (section 72AA).** A renter must give written notice as soon as practicable of damage or a breakdown of facilities, fixtures or equipment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). That is the "report" the retaliation clause refers to [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Valid form (section 91ZZO).** A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed, and gives its reason or reasons. It must also state the termination date [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Deadline to challenge.** For fixed-term end notices, you can't apply to the Tribunal after 28 days (term of 6 months or more) or 21 days (term under 6 months) [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). I found no deadline in these excerpts for a month-to-month tenancy.

## What you can check and ask
1. **Which section and reason the notice gives.** Check that it is in the prescribed form, signed, addressed to you, and gives a specific reason and termination date [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The later prescribed form says a notice must explain why it was given, with specific details [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Whether it is a retaliation case.** Compare the dates of your repair request and the notice. The prescribed form lists "you tried to exercise your rights as a renter" as a reason to challenge a notice at VCAT [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Whether your repair request was in writing.** For non-urgent repairs, you can ask the Director to investigate if the provider hasn't done the repairs within 14 days of written notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). You can also apply to the Tribunal [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
4. **Urgent repairs.** If the leaks are urgent, you can apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring the repairs, which the Tribunal must hear within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
5. **Time limits.** Act quickly, because challenge deadlines exist [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The form advises seeking advice immediately from a community legal organisation or Consumer Affairs Victoria (1300 558 181) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
6. **You don't have to leave on the notice date.** If you stay, the provider must apply to VCAT for a possession order, and only Victoria Police can carry out a forced eviction under a VCAT warrant [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**Gap:** the documents don't include the version in force on 1 November 2019, so I can't confirm any of the above for that date.

must-mention.reason: The answer fails because it omits two of the three required points. It never says a no-reason notice is allowed with at least 120 days' notice, and it never says the tenant can challenge at VCAT within 60 days; it instead says 'I found no deadline in these excerpts for a month-to-month tenancy.' It does partly cover the retaliation point by noting that notices 'have no effect if they were given in response to the renter exercising... a right under the Act', but it hedges on whether this applies to a month-to-month renter.

must-not-say.reason: No. The answer's checklist effectively tells the user the landlord needed to give a reason: "Check that it is in the prescribed form, signed, addressed to you, and gives a specific reason and termination date." It caveats that its sources are later versions of the Act, but this item is presented as something to check on the user's own notice. That conveys a reason requirement for the 2019 month-to-month notice rather than limiting it to a later date. (The 28/21-day deadlines are expressly limited to fixed-term notices, so the deadline criterion alone would not fail.)

version-cited.reason: No. The answer never names the required Residential Tenancies Act 1997 Authorised Version No. 088 (2 July 2019). It instead presents rules and steps from versions not in force on 1 November 2019: "rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf" (v101), the 97-109aa110 link (version 110), and the Regulations at 21-3sra002. It does this despite caveats, and deleting that material would remove the answer's substance.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
**Version applied:** You are asking on 1 October 2025, so I used *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf" (6 August 2025). The file name indicates Authorised Version 110. The next version in the documents is v111, dated 25 November 2025, so it was not in force on your date.

## What the law says

- **Fixed advertised rent.** A rental provider or agent must not advertise or offer a property unless the rent is advertised or offered as a fixed amount. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **No inviting higher offers.** They must not "solicit or otherwise invite an offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount." The same penalties apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **False or misleading rent advertising.** They must not make a false or misleading representation about the rent when promoting or advertising the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Gap: accepting an uninvited higher offer.** Version 110 only bans *soliciting or inviting* higher offers [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A separate ban on *accepting* an unsolicited higher offer (s 30F(4)) appears only in v111 (25 November 2025) and later [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It is not in the version in force on 1 October 2025. If the other applicant offered more without being asked, the documents do not show that accepting it was prohibited on your date.
- **The "withdrawn" email.** Nothing in the retrieved version says what happens when an agent wrongly records an application as withdrawn. The nearest provisions are:
  - s 30E bans misleading or deceptive conduct that induces someone to enter a rental agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). It is aimed at inducing people to *enter* agreements, so it may not fit your facts well.
  - s 30A bans refusing to let premises on the basis of a protected attribute under the *Equal Opportunity Act 2010* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask the agent in writing** why your application was recorded as withdrawn, and whether higher offers were invited, for example in the listing or by the agent. That matters because inviting them is prohibited [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Check the listing.** If the higher rent was invited or advertised inconsistently, that could breach s 30F or s 30G [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Compensation for discrimination.** If you think the real reason was a protected attribute, s 210AA lets you apply to the Tribunal for compensation for loss caused by discrimination [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Tribunal orders for misleading conduct.** The Act says s 472(1A) provides for Tribunal orders where s 30E is contravened [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text does not set out what those orders are.
- **Gaps in the documents.** They do not say which body handles a s 30F complaint, what remedy a renter gets for a breach, or whether a withdrawn application can be reinstated. I won't guess at those.

## What to save as evidence

The documents contain no evidence checklist for this situation. Based on the elements above, these records would be useful:

- Your application and its submission confirmation, with dates and times.
- The "withdrawn" email, with full headers and sender details.
- Any messages or call notes showing you did not withdraw.
- Screenshots of the original listing at the advertised price and the new, higher listing, with dates.
- Anything showing the agent invited higher offers, such as listing wording or messages.
- Any information about the other offer, and who told you about it.

must-mention.reason: No: the answer never states that relisting at a higher fixed rent is lawful by itself. It only says that if the higher rent was 'invited or advertised inconsistently, that could breach s 30F or s 30G', which implies the point without stating it. The other three points are covered: inviting higher offers is banned, accepting an unsolicited offer was not banned on 1 October 2025 ('the documents do not show that accepting it was prohibited on your date'), and 'Nothing in the retrieved version says what happens when an agent wrongly records an application as withdrawn.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the three claims is asserted. Relisting is only a possible breach "if the higher rent was invited or advertised inconsistently". Accepting an unsolicited higher offer is said to be banned "only in v111 (25 November 2025) and later" and "not in the version in force on 1 October 2025". On forcing the agent to rent, the answer says the documents do not say "whether a withdrawn application can be reinstated".

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as Authorised Version 110 ('rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf', 6 August 2025, links 97-109aa110) and applies ss 30F and 30G from that version; it mentions v111's s 30F(4) only to say that rule was not in force on 1 October 2025 and does not rely on it.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
## What the law says

I've applied *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf"). It is the version in force on 15 October 2026. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

- **Consent is needed, but it can't be unreasonably refused.** A renter may keep a pet with the provider's written consent or a Tribunal order. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The provider "must not unreasonably refuse to consent". [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Your request must be in the right form.** It must be in the form approved by the Director and given to the residential rental provider. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) You say you used the official form. The documents don't say whether giving it to the agent counts as giving it to the provider.
- **A refusal alone isn't enough, because of the 14-day rule.** The provider is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days of being given the request, they apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) under section 71D. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **What the provider asks VCAT for.** The provider can apply for an order that it is reasonable to refuse consent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Tribunal can instead order that you may keep the pet. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) It can only order refusal or exclusion if it is satisfied that refusal is reasonable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **What VCAT may consider.** These include the type of pet, the character and nature of the premises, the appliances, fixtures and fittings, and whether refusal is permitted under any Act. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) They also include any prescribed matters and any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## Applying it to you

- **Timing.** You sent the request three weeks ago, which is 21 days. The 14-day window has passed. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Deemed consent.** If the owner or agent did not apply to VCAT within those 14 days, the owner is taken to have consented, even though the agent said no. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents don't tell me whether an application was made, so you would need to check that.
- **The allergy.** The Act doesn't list an owner's allergy as a ground for refusal. It would fall under "any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant". [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The documents don't say whether an allergy would be a reasonable ground when the owner rarely visits, so I can't say how VCAT would decide. That the owner hardly ever visits seems relevant to the character of the premises and their use, but this is my inference, not something stated in the documents.

## What you can do

1. **Ask whether the provider applied to VCAT within 14 days of your request.** If not, the Act treats consent as given. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
2. **Put this in writing to the agent**, citing sections 71C(1) and 71C(2). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
3. **Be aware of the risk if you bring the dog in without a VCAT order or written consent.** The provider can apply to VCAT to exclude the pet. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) A notice to vacate for a pet kept without consent is only available if VCAT has ordered the pet excluded, at least 14 days have passed since the order took effect, and you haven't complied. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) That notice must give a date at least 28 days after it is given. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The documents don't cover how to apply to VCAT yourself, or what the Director-approved form looks like. For personal advice, you could contact a tenancy advice service.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The 'provider is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days of being given the request, they apply to the Tribunal (VCAT)'. It applies this to the 21 days elapsed: 'If the owner or agent did not apply to VCAT within those 14 days, the owner is taken to have consented'. The next step is to 'Ask whether the provider applied to VCAT within 14 days' and 'Put this in writing to the agent'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the failing claims are made: the answer says "A refusal alone isn't enough, because of the 14-day rule" and that the provider is "taken to have consented" unless it applies to VCAT, it puts the duty to apply on the provider rather than the renter, and on the allergy it says "I can't say how VCAT would decide."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the required document with its in-force version ('Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026', file 'rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf'), and every citation links to 97-109aa115, so no rule comes from a version that was not in force on 15 October 2026.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Version applied:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", dated 6 August 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). It is the latest document dated on or before 1 October 2025. The excerpt I retrieved doesn't print an "Authorised Version No." line, so "v110" comes from the file name. The two later versions are dated 25 November 2025 (v111) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and 13 October 2026 (v115) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). They were not in force on 1 October 2025.

## What the law says

- **The notice stays in force until it is withdrawn in writing.** A notice to vacate is withdrawn "only if a notice of withdrawal is given". That withdrawal must be in writing and signed by both the person who gave the notice and the person who received it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The landlord has not withdrawn it, so it is still in force.
- **The buyer pulling out does not cancel the notice on its face.** The retrieved text has no rule that a sale notice lapses when a buyer withdraws, so I can't say it does.
- **A notice can be based on the premises being "sold or offered for sale with vacant possession".** Section 91ZZB(1) lets a landlord give a notice if the premises are, immediately after the termination date, "to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The landlord may say they will re-list the property.
- **The notice period was 60 days.** Under s 91ZZB(4) in the 6 August 2025 version, the termination date must be "not less than 60 days" after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The 90-day period appears only in the later 25 November 2025 version [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), so it does not apply to a notice assessed under the law as at 1 October 2025.
- **Validity requirements.** A notice is not valid unless it meets these requirements [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf):
  - It is in the prescribed form, addressed to the renter and signed.
  - It states the reason.
  - It is accompanied by supporting documentary evidence.
  - It states the termination date.
- **A landlord who gets possession can't re-let for 6 months.** If the landlord obtains possession after a notice under s 91ZZB, they must not re-let the premises primarily as a residence for 6 months after the notice date. The penalty is 150 penalty units for an individual and 750 for a company. There are exceptions, including where the Tribunal determines the premises may be let [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the landlord to withdraw the notice in writing.** Both you and the landlord must sign it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
2. **Challenge the notice at the Tribunal.** Before or at the hearing of a possession order application, you can apply to challenge the notice's validity. You must apply within 30 days after the notice was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can decide whether the notice is valid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Check your notice date now, as this window may be closing or may have passed.
3. **Check the notice for defects.** Look at the form, signature, stated reason, evidence and the 60-day period [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
4. **You can leave early if you choose.** A renter who has received a s 91ZZB notice can give a notice of intention to vacate with a termination date at least 14 days away, even during a fixed term [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

The retrieved text refers to applications for possession orders [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), but it doesn't set out the full process for them. It also doesn't say whether a collapsed sale makes a notice invalid, or what the Tribunal would decide in your case. Whether you must leave therefore turns on whether the notice is valid and whether the landlord obtains a possession order. A tenant advocacy service or the Tribunal can advise on that.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered, including the hardest one, the dependence on the notice's ground and evidence. The answer quotes the s 91ZZB(1) ground "to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession", says "The landlord may say they will re-list the property", and requires that the notice "states the reason" and is "accompanied by supporting documentary evidence". It also gives the 60-day minimum period, says withdrawal must be "in writing and signed by both" parties, and lists next steps: ask for a signed written withdrawal or challenge the notice at the Tribunal within 30 days.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer asserts none of the three failure conditions: it states 'The buyer pulling out does not cancel the notice on its face', that withdrawal must be 'signed by both the person who gave the notice and the person who received it', and that the termination date must be 'not less than 60 days' after notice, mentioning 90 days only to say it 'does not apply to a notice assessed under the law as at 1 October 2025'.

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 with its version as "file 'rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf', dated 6 August 2025" and links 97-109aa110, and every rule it applies is cited to that version, mentioning the later v111 (25 November 2025) 90-day period only to say it does not apply on 1 October 2025.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
## What the law says

**Document used:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", dated 6 August 2025, Authorised Version No. 110. The version number comes from the file title. This is the latest Act version I retrieved that predates 1 October 2025.

- A residential rental provider must give the renter **at least 60 days' notice, in the prescribed form**, of a proposed rent increase (s 44(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The notice must state the amount of the increase, how it was calculated, and the renter's right to ask the Director to investigate within 30 days (s 44(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **A rent increase that contravenes s 44 is invalid** (s 44(5)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The rent also cannot go up at intervals of less than 12 months (s 44(4A)). In a fixed-term agreement, it can only go up if the agreement allows it (s 44(4)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## Your situation

- **Do you have to pay the higher rent?** On the Act as it stood on 1 October 2025, an email from the agent is not a prescribed-form notice. You said you never got an official notice. An increase made without one contravenes s 44, so it is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Based on the documents, you aren't required to pay the higher rent.
- **From when?** No date applies yet. The 60 days run from when a valid notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The earliest a valid increase could start is 60 days after you receive a proper notice. It must also respect the 12-month and fixed-term limits above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Ask the agent in writing for a proper prescribed-form notice.** Ask them to confirm that the increase can't start until a valid notice has been given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check your agreement and the date of your last increase.** If it is a fixed term, the increase must be allowed by the agreement. There must also be at least 12 months since the last increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
3. **Once you receive a valid notice, you can challenge it if you think the rent is excessive:**
   - Apply in writing to the Director within 30 days after the notice is given, and the Director must investigate and report (ss 45(1)(b), 45(2), 45(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
   - After the report, apply to the Tribunal within 30 days of receiving it (s 46(1)–(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
**Version used:** Residential Tenancies Act 1997, "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf" (Authorised Version No. 115, dated 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This is the version in force on 15 October 2026. I take the version number from the file name, because the retrieved pages don't show the cover page.

## What the law says

- **Damage:** A renter and any visitor must not intentionally or negligently damage the rented premises. Fair wear and tear isn't counted as damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether your dog's chewing is "negligent" damage or not isn't something the documents decide.
- **You must tell the owner in writing.** A renter who becomes aware of damage must give the rental provider written notice "as soon as practicable". The notice must say that the damage happened and what it is [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Section 72AA also requires written notice of damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Email is allowed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). So the Act doesn't let you keep quiet about it.
- **Who does the repair is the owner's choice.** If damage results from a renter's failure to take care, the provider may give a written repair notice. The provider can choose one of two options [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):
  1. Require you to repair it at your expense within 14 days. If it isn't repaired "in a tradesman-like manner" in that time, the provider may repair it at your expense.
  2. Say the provider is doing the repairs, and you are liable for the reasonable cost.
- **Cost:** If the provider does the repairs, you owe the reasonable cost once you're given the particulars in writing. You must pay within 14 days after the repairs are completed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can ask the Tribunal for an extension if you can't pay in time. If you're in hardship, you can give written notice that you need an extra 14 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Moving out:** At the end of the agreement you must leave the premises in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Who may do repairs:** The standard-form agreement in the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 says "Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs—both urgent and non-urgent" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The only version I retrieved is dated 25 November 2025 ("rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf"). I can't confirm from the documents that no later version applies on 15 October 2026.

## What you can do

1. **Give written notice of the damage now.** Email is enough. Describe the damage to the skirting boards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Offer to repair it, or ask the owner how they want it handled.** Ask them to confirm in writing. That fits the process in section 78, where the owner decides whether you repair it or they do [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **If you use a tradesperson, use a suitably qualified one** [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Keep the invoice and photos. Do this after you've told the owner, not instead of telling them.
4. **Check pet consent.** A renter may keep a pet only with the provider's written consent or a Tribunal order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether you had that.

## Insurance

The documents I retrieved don't say whether damage you caused, or a repair done without telling the owner, would affect the owner's insurance. I can't answer that from them. The owner or their insurer would need to answer it, and your own policy, if you have contents or liability cover, might also be relevant.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found contain no rule on how many circuits a rental needs. They also say nothing about a circuit being overloaded or tripping when two appliances run together.

## What the law says

**Document used:** *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf", dated 1 June 2022, Authorised Version v002 (the number comes from the file name). It is the latest regulations version I retrieved that predates 1 March 2023. I did not retrieve a v003, so I can't rule out an intervening version.

- **Electrical safety standard (Schedule 4, cl 9):** "On and from 29 March 2023", all power outlets and lighting circuits must connect to a switchboard-type circuit breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000. They must also connect to a switchboard-type residual current device (RCD) complying with the listed standards [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Timing:** On 1 March 2023 this standard had not yet started, because it begins on 29 March 2023 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Later versions repeat the same wording [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), but they are dated after your question.
- **What it doesn't cover:** The clause is about breaker and RCD protection. It does not set a minimum number of circuits, a minimum capacity, or how power points are divided between circuits [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **The Act:** The only versions of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* I retrieved are v111 (25 November 2025) [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and v115 (13 October 2026) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Both postdate 1 March 2023, so I can't say what the Act required on that date. I haven't relied on them.

## What you can ask for

The v002 regulations include a standard-form agreement. The excerpt I retrieved appears to be the form for agreements of more than 5 years, and I did not retrieve v002's text of the other form. Under that form, you can:

- **Request a repair in writing.** Notify the rental provider in writing of damage or of a breakdown of facilities, fixtures or equipment they supplied. They must carry out non-urgent repairs "in a reasonable time" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Go to VCAT.** You may apply to VCAT for an order if the repairs haven't been done within 14 days of notice [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Ask for the electrical safety check date.** The form requires an electrical safety check of provider-supplied installations, appliances and fittings every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician. You can ask for the date of the latest check in writing [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs probably don't apply.** The form lists failure of an essential service or appliance for hot water, cooking, heating or laundering supplied by the rental provider. A breaker tripping from combined load doesn't clearly fit that description [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

Whether a circuit that trips under normal use counts as "good repair" is not answered in the documents I retrieved. I can't say your provider is obliged to add circuits. From 29 March 2023, you could ask them to confirm the switchboard has compliant circuit breakers and RCDs [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?

## What the law says

I relied on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", dated 13 October 2026. This is the version in force on 15 October 2026. The retrieved text doesn't print an "Authorised Version" number. The only number I can give is "v115" from the file name.

- **Utility charges.** The Act lets an operator charge separately for electricity, gas and water only for a separately metered room, and only where the operator pays for them. That charge can't be more than the supplier's charge [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This is about your own room, so it doesn't clearly cover a shared laundry.
- **Public and community housing.** If your house is run by Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, it can impose a service charge for "laundry… services or facilities". This applies only if it isn't possible or practicable to accurately measure your use. The charge must not exceed the cost of providing the service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). My reading is that a coin slot measures use, so this provision may not fit. The documents don't say so directly.
- **Washing machines.** The standards regulations require a washing machine for every 12 or fewer residents from 26 February 2024. They don't say whether it must be free [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). The retrieved copy of those regulations is dated 1 December 2024, so I can't confirm it is the version in force today.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I retrieved don't confirm that the advertising ban was in force on 1 October 2025. A photo of mould also doesn't prove by itself that the place fails the minimum standards.

## What the law says

**Which versions applied on 1 October 2025**
- The Act version in force was *rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf* (Residential Tenancies Act 1997, version 110, dated 6 August 2025) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The Regulations version was *rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf* (Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 4, dated 1 July 2025) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- I'm taking the version numbers from the file names. The excerpts don't print an "Authorised Version" label.

**Is the ad allowed?**
- Version 110 has s 65A, which requires the rental provider to make sure the premises meet the prescribed rental minimum standards by the day the renter moves in [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- Version 110 has no section on advertising. Section 65A is followed directly by s 66 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- A rule against advertising premises that don't meet the standards (s 65B) appears only in later versions. These are *rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf* (25 November 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf* (13 October 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Those later versions say the provider or agent must not advertise or offer premises unless they reasonably believe the premises comply with the standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Version 111 shows s 65B as inserted by Act No. 6/2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say when it started, so I can't say it applied on 1 October 2025.
- I can't tell you that this ad breached the law on that date. I haven't relied on anything outside the documents.

**Does the photo prove non-compliance?**
- The mould standard says each room must be "free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" (Schedule 4, clause 8) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- Bedrooms are covered, because the standard applies to each room [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- A photo shows that mould is present. The standard also depends on the mould being caused by or related to the building structure. A photo alone doesn't show that.
- The documents don't say what evidence is needed or who has to prove non-compliance. I can't say how much a photo would count for.

## What the renter can do or ask

- **Ask for urgent repairs.** If the premises don't meet the standards on or immediately after the day the renter moves in, the renter may issue a request to the provider for urgent repairs to bring them up to standard (s 65A(2)) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Rely on the general repair duty.** The provider must keep the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation (s 68(1)) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask for substantiation (later version only).** Version 111 lets the Director require a provider or agent to substantiate claims made about rented premises before a rental agreement is entered (s 510L). The Director can do this by a written notice, and the provider has 21 days to respond [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). This provision isn't in the version 110 excerpt, so I can't confirm it applied on 1 October 2025.
- **Public warnings (later version only).** Version 111 also lets the Minister or Director issue a public warning about premises offered for residential occupation (s 510K) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The same caveat applies.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
## What the law says

The source is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", dated 13 October 2026). That is the latest version dated before 15 October 2026. The version number comes from the file name, because the retrieved text doesn't print an "Authorised Version" number.

- **You need written consent.** A renter must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the rented premises without the rental provider's written consent (s 81(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Without consent it is invalid.** An assignment or sub-letting without consent is invalid unless the Tribunal has determined that consent isn't required (s 81(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The agent can act against you.** If you have assigned, sub-let, or "purported to" assign or sub-let any part of the premises without consent, the rental provider may give you a notice to vacate (s 91ZV(1)). The termination date must be at least 14 days after the notice is given (s 91ZV(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **If you don't leave.** The rental provider may apply to VCAT for a possession order [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) (Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Form 6, version dated 30 June 2026).

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask for consent.** If you would rather your friend stayed, you can ask the agent for written consent. The rental provider must not unreasonably withhold consent, and can't refuse on the basis of an attribute in section 6 of the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 (s 81(2), (2A)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The provider can't charge a fee for giving consent (s 84(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Apply to the Tribunal if consent is refused.** If consent is withheld and you think that is unreasonable, you can apply to the Tribunal for a determination that consent isn't required (s 82) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Expect inspections.** The agent can enter on 24 hours' written notice if it has reasonable grounds to believe you have breached your duties under the Act or the agreement (ss 85(b)(iii), 86(1)(e)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

The retrieved documents don't say how a renter can make a friend leave. They have no steps, notice period or process for a renter removing an occupant. They also don't say whether simply letting a friend stay, as opposed to a paid sub-letting, counts as "sub-letting" under s 81 or s 91ZV. I can't answer those points from the documents. For your own situation, check the tenancy agreement and speak to Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advice service.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
# Your rental application and the higher rent (as at 1 October 2025)

The version in force on 1 October 2025 was the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 file **rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf** (dated 6 August 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The next version in the documents is dated 25 November 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). I take v110 as the version in force on your date, because it is the latest one dated before then. The text I retrieved doesn't print an "Authorised Version No." itself, so "110" comes from the file name.

## What the law says

- **Fixed rent.** Under s 30F(1), a provider or agent must not advertise or offer premises unless the rent is advertised or offered as a fixed amount. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **No inviting higher offers.** Under s 30F(3), a provider or agent must not "solicit or otherwise invite an offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount." The same penalties apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **False or misleading rent claims.** Under s 30G(2), a provider or agent who promotes or advertises premises must not make a false or misleading representation about the rent. This applies to providers and agents not acting in trade or commerce, and it doesn't limit the Australian Consumer Law (Victoria) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Misleading conduct.** Under s 30E, a provider or agent must not induce someone to enter a rental agreement by misleading or deceptive conduct, or by a false representation about the rent payable. A note says s 472(1A) lets the Tribunal make orders for a contravention of s 30E [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Discrimination.** If the "withdrawal" was really a refusal based on a protected attribute, s 30A prohibits it. A note to that section says you may apply to the Tribunal for compensation for loss caused by discrimination (s 210AA) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**Accepting an unsolicited higher offer.** On 1 October 2025, v110 did not contain a ban on accepting an unsolicited higher offer. The only bidding rule in it was the ban on soliciting or inviting higher offers (s 30F(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A ban on accepting an unsolicited or uninvited higher offer (s 30F(4)) first appears in the later version dated 25 November 2025, where it is marked as inserted by No. 6/2025 s 7 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). I can't attribute it to the law as it stood on your date.

## What you can do or ask

- **Challenge the "withdrawn" email.** The documents contain no rule about an agent recording an application as withdrawn. They also don't say how a dispute like that is resolved. You can still ask the agent in writing to correct the record and to confirm whether your application at the advertised rent is still live.
- **Ask whether anyone invited a higher offer.** If the agent or provider solicited or invited the higher offer, that would contravene s 30F(3) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Hearing that "someone offered more" isn't enough on its own. Under the v110 text, what matters is whether the offer was invited.
- **Ask about the new rent.** You can ask why the listing rose after your application. A false or misleading statement about the rent could engage s 30G(2), and s 30E applies if it was used to induce someone to enter an agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Tribunal or complaint route.** The retrieved text doesn't set out how to lodge a complaint or what remedies apply to s 30F or s 30G. The only Tribunal remedies it points to are the s 472(1A) note for s 30E and compensation for discrimination under s 210AA [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). For anything beyond that, I can't say from these documents.

## What to save as evidence

The documents don't list evidence to keep. This is practical advice tied to the points above:

- Your application and any confirmation of it, showing the advertised rent and the date.
- The "withdrawn" email, with full headers and timestamp, and any reply you send.
- Screenshots or archived copies of the original advertisement and the new listing, with dates and prices.
- All messages with the agent (emails, texts, call logs, portal messages), especially any that mention other offers, bidding, or "best offers."
- Anything showing you did not withdraw, such as portal history or messages confirming your interest.
- Anything the agent or provider said about why the rent changed.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
**Version applied:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 (file rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It is the version in force on 15 October 2026.

## What the law says

- A landlord (the "residential rental provider") **must not unreasonably refuse** consent to a renter keeping a pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- A "no" from the agent doesn't end the matter. The provider is **taken to have consented** unless, **within 14 days** of being given the request, they **apply to the Tribunal (VCAT)** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The provider can ask the Tribunal for an order that refusing consent is reasonable. The Tribunal can instead order that the renter may keep the pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- If the Tribunal is satisfied refusal is reasonable, it can order that refusal is reasonable and can exclude the pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The Tribunal "may have regard to" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):
  - the type of pet;
  - the character and nature of the premises;
  - the appliances, fixtures and fittings;
  - whether refusing is permitted under any Act;
  - any prescribed matters;
  - any other matter it considers relevant.

## Applied to your situation

- **Timing:** You sent the request three weeks ago, which is more than 14 days. If neither the owner nor the agent applied to VCAT within those 14 days, the Act treats the owner as having consented, whatever the agent said [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't tell me whether an application was made, so you need to check.
- **The allergy:** The Act doesn't list an owner's allergy as a ground for refusal. It also doesn't say whether the owner rarely visiting matters. Those would fall under the Tribunal's discretion to consider "any other matter … relevant" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I can't say from the documents how VCAT would decide.
- **Who received the request:** The Act says the renter must give the request to the residential rental provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether giving it to the agent counts. Check that it reached the owner or was properly passed on.

## What you can do

1. Ask the agent and owner in writing whether they applied to VCAT within 14 days of your request, and when.
2. If they didn't, point to the Act's deemed-consent rule [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Act also says a renter may keep a pet with the provider's written consent or a Tribunal order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say how deemed consent compares with written consent, so you may want to ask for written confirmation.
3. If they did apply, VCAT will decide. You can put forward points such as the owner rarely visiting, since the Tribunal may consider other relevant matters [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. Don't ignore a Tribunal order excluding the pet. The Act's contents list includes a section on notice to vacate when a pet is kept without consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The only text I retrieved for that section is from an earlier version, *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 111 (25 November 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). It allows a notice to vacate if you haven't complied at least 14 days after the exclusion order took effect, with at least 28 days' notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). I haven't seen the current wording.

The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (version dated 30 June 2026) say only that a renter must seek consent and the provider must not unreasonably refuse [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The retrieved excerpt doesn't show an Authorised Version number for them.

Point 2 (the hardest) is applied to the facts: 'You sent the request three weeks ago, which is more than 14 days. If neither the owner nor the agent applied to VCAT within those 14 days, the Act treats the owner as having consented, whatever the agent said.' Point 3: 'Ask the agent and owner in writing whether they applied to VCAT within 14 days of your request.'

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
# Notice to vacate for sale: do you still have to leave?

**Short answer:** The documents I retrieved don't say a sale notice lapses automatically when the buyer withdraws. A notice can only be withdrawn by a signed written notice of withdrawal, according to the 2019 versions of the Act. The text I could see of the version in force on 1 October 2025 doesn't confirm this. The landlord would still need a VCAT possession order to make you leave.

## What the law says

**Version applied:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", dated 6 August 2025 (version 110, going by the file name) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This is the latest retrieved version dated on or before 1 October 2025. The later versions are dated 25 November 2025 and 13 October 2026, so they don't apply to your date [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

- **Ground for the notice (s 91ZZB):** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are, immediately after the termination date, "to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This ground is about selling or offering for sale, not about a particular buyer. The Act says nothing in these sections about a buyer pulling out.
- **Timing and notice period:** If there is a contract of sale, the notice must be given within 14 days after it is signed. If the contract has conditions, it must be given within 14 days after the last condition is satisfied. The notice must give a termination date at least **60 days** after it is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). (The later versions, dated 25 November 2025 and 13 October 2026, show this changed to 90 days. That is not the law for your date [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).)
- **Withdrawal:** I found the text of s 91ZZQ only in the 2019 versions: "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf" (2 July 2019) and "rta-1997-v089-2019-12-04.pdf" (4 December 2019) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf). It says a notice to vacate "is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given". That notice must be in writing, signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person it was given to [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The retrieved parts of the 2025 version don't include that section, so I can't confirm it is unchanged for 1 October 2025.
- **If you don't leave:** The landlord must apply to VCAT for a possession order. VCAT decides whether the landlord was entitled to give the notice, and makes the order only if it is satisfied that it is reasonable and proportionate. Only Victoria Police can carry out a forced eviction, and only under a VCAT warrant [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the landlord to withdraw the notice.** Request a written notice of withdrawal that both of you sign (see s 91ZZQ above) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Challenge the notice at VCAT.** The prescribed form lists reasons you may challenge a notice, including that it wasn't given properly or that the reason given is incorrect or incomplete. You can also challenge its validity if the landlord applies for a possession order [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The 2019 versions allowed a challenge application within 30 days of the notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). I couldn't confirm that limit for the 2025 version, so check your deadline quickly.
3. **Leave early if you want to.** A renter given a sale notice can give a notice of intention to vacate with at least **14 days'** notice. No lease break fee applies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
4. **Get advice.** The form suggests contacting a community legal organisation listed on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website, or calling 1300 558 181 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**Not covered:** The documents don't say whether a failed sale makes the notice invalid. They also don't say whether VCAT would treat the buyer pulling out as a reason to refuse a possession order.

It quotes the 'to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession' ground and separately notes the 14-day timing rule when there is a contract, but it never says the answer turns on which ground the notice relied on. The other points are covered: the 60-day minimum, withdrawal 'only if a notice of withdrawal is given' in writing signed by both, and next steps such as asking for a signed withdrawal or challenging at VCAT.

- The rental provider must give you **at least 60 days notice, in the prescribed form**, of a proposed rent increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The notice can cover **only one** increase. It must state the amount and how it was calculated. It must also tell you about your right to ask the Director to investigate within 30 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The rent can't be increased at intervals of **less than 12 months** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- In a fixed term agreement, the rent can't go up before the term ends unless the agreement provides for an increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **A rent increase that breaks these rules is invalid** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## From when?
- **An email without a valid notice gives no start date.** An increase that breaches s 44 is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The agent refusing to negotiate doesn't change that.
- **The earliest the higher rent can apply** is 60 days after a valid prescribed-form notice is given, and only if the 12-month and fixed-term rules are also met [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do
1. **Keep paying your current rent** and ask the agent in writing for a valid notice. This is my practical suggestion, not something the documents say.
2. **Once you get a valid notice, you can challenge it as excessive.** You have 30 days after the notice is given to apply in writing to the Director to investigate and report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
3. **After the Director's report,** you can apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) within 30 days of receiving it for an order declaring the rent excessive [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
4. **If you skip the Director,** you can apply to VCAT directly, but only after the 30 days have passed and with VCAT's leave. VCAT can grant leave if you have reasonable grounds for not asking the Director [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

No. 123/2025. The Act version I used says 60 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I can't tell from these documents whether 90 days applied on 1 October 2025, so check this.

I can't confirm that rule applied on 1 October 2025.
