question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
## What the law says

I used the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* in the document titled "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", dated 13 October 2026. It is labelled v115 and is the version in force on 15 October 2026. The documents don't give a separate "Authorised Version" number, so v115 comes from the file name.

- **You must not damage the property.** A renter must not intentionally or negligently damage the rented premises. Fair wear and tear doesn't count as damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 61).
- **You must tell the owner in writing.** A renter who becomes aware of damage must give written notice "as soon as practicable". The notice must say that the damage happened and what it is [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 62). Section 72AA repeats the duty to report damage in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Email is allowed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **You must leave the property in its original condition.** At the end of the tenancy, the premises must be left in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 63(2)).
- **The owner can require a repair.** If the damage came from a breach of s 61(1), the owner can give you a written repair notice. It can require you to repair at your own expense within 14 days. If you haven't repaired it "in a proper and tradesman-like manner" by then, the owner can repair it and you are liable for the reasonable cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (ss 78–79). The owner can instead say they are doing the repairs themselves, and you are then liable for the reasonable cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (ss 78(2)(d), 79(2)). You must reimburse the owner within 14 days after the repairs are completed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 79(4)). You can ask the Tribunal for an extension if you can't pay in time [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 79(5)). If you are in hardship, you can give written notice that you need an additional 14 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 79(6)).

## Can you just get someone to fix it without telling the owner?

**You shouldn't skip telling them.** The Act requires written notice of damage as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text doesn't say you are banned from repairing it yourself first. It does contemplate you repairing at your own expense, but in a "proper and tradesman-like manner" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Quietly fixing it still leaves you in breach of the notice duty.

Chewed skirting boards are also not an urgent repair. The urgent-repairs rules cover things like a burst water service, a gas leak or flood damage [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do:**
1. Send written notice (email is fine) describing the damage now, ideally with photos. Photos taken at the start and end of a tenancy are encouraged [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
2. Offer to arrange and pay for a tradesperson to repair it, and ask the owner to agree. The Tribunal considers whether the owner was notified and given a reasonable opportunity to carry out repairs, and whether there is documentary evidence of the repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 75(4)). Keeping receipts and photos helps.
3. The Form 2 agreement text (for tenancies of more than 5 years) says only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I can't tell from the documents whether your agreement uses that form.

## Would it affect the owner's insurance?

**The documents I retrieved don't answer this.** They contain nothing about the owner's insurance, whether a repair affects a claim, or whether telling or not telling the owner has insurance consequences. I can't say either way. The owner or their insurer would need to answer that.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. The hardest one, renter responsibility, is met by stating that 'A renter must not intentionally or negligently damage the rented premises. Fair wear and tear doesn't count as damage' and that 'the premises must be left in the same condition as when you moved in', with the owner able to require repair at the renter's expense. The answer also covers written notice 'as soon as practicable', says 'The documents I retrieved don't answer this' on insurance, and gives next steps such as sending written notice and offering to pay for repairs.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer rejects a quiet repair ("You shouldn't skip telling them" and "Quietly fixing it still leaves you in breach of the notice duty"), states no insurance outcome ("I can't say either way"), and never says the renter must pay the owner's insurance excess.

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the Act as "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf" (v115) and identifies the Regulations through the link "21-3sra009" (version 009), and both are the versions in force on 15 October 2026, so no rule it applies comes from another version.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
## What the law says (as at 1 March 2023)

I used the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021**, file *rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf*, dated 1 June 2022 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). It is the only retrieved version that predates 1 March 2023. The filename shows "v002", but the retrieved text doesn't print an "Authorised Version No.", so I can't quote one. The other retrieved versions are dated 2025 and 2026, so they post-date your question and I haven't relied on them.

- **The documents set no minimum number of circuits.** Schedule 4 (Rental minimum standards), clause 9 deals with electrical safety. It requires all power outlets and lighting circuits to be connected to a switchboard-type circuit breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000. They must also be connected to a switchboard-type residual current device (RCD) complying with one of the listed standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Clause 9 wasn't in force yet on 1 March 2023.** It applies "on and from 29 March 2023" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Nothing in clause 9 says how many circuits a rental needs or how power points must be spread across them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Maintenance duties apply now.** The rental provider must ensure the premises meet the rental minimum standards. They must also maintain the premises in good repair and in a fit condition for occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## What you can ask for

- **An electrical safety check record.** The rental provider must have all electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provide checked every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician. On your request, they must give you the date of the most recent check in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If no check was done in the 2 years before you moved in, they must arrange one as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **A repair request in writing.** Tell the rental provider in writing about a breakdown of facilities, fixtures or equipment they supplied. They must do non-urgent repairs in a reasonable time. If they haven't done them within 14 days of your notice, you can apply to VCAT for an order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs.** The form lists failure of an essential service or appliance for hot water, cooking, heating or laundering supplied by the rental provider. It refers to section 3(1) of the Act for the full definition [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). That section isn't in the retrieved documents. So I can't say whether a repeatedly tripping breaker counts as urgent.

## What the documents don't answer

They don't say whether a breaker tripping under a kettle-plus-heater load is a breach or a repair issue. They also don't say you can demand extra circuits. The most they support is asking for the electrical safety check date and putting a written repair request to the rental provider. For a firmer answer, check the Act itself or contact Consumer Affairs Victoria.

must-mention.reason: Both points are covered. Point 1 is met by 'The documents set no minimum number of circuits' and 'Nothing in clause 9 says how many circuits a rental needs', which the rubric accepts as equivalent to there being no rule. Point 2 is met by the advice to ask the rental provider for 'the date of the most recent check in writing' and to put a 'repair request in writing'. The answer also discusses urgent repairs; any one of the listed alternatives would be enough.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer states "The documents set no minimum number of circuits" and "Clause 9 wasn't in force yet on 1 March 2023. It applies 'on and from 29 March 2023'," so it neither sets a minimum number of circuits nor says sharing a circuit is illegal, and it does not claim the circuit breaker/RCD standard already applies on the question date.

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names the Regulations in force on that date ('rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf', link '21-3sra002', i.e. Authorised Version No. 002), but it never names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 with a version: it refers only to 'section 3(1) of the Act' and says 'check the Act itself', omitting Authorised Version No. 101.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't say whether a rooming house operator may charge for coin-operated washing machines. The Act does regulate how service charges are handled.

**Source used:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", dated 13 October 2026 (the file metadata shows 14 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This is the latest version retrieved before 15 October 2026. The excerpt doesn't print the words "Authorised Version No.", so "version 115" comes from the file name only.

## What the law says

- **Utility charges (s 108):** An operator may charge for electricity, gas and water used in a room, but only if the room is separately metered and the operator pays the supplier. The charge can't exceed the supplier's charge [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This covers a resident's own room, not a shared laundry.
- **Service charges (s 109):** If an operator charges for services, it must do two things [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):
  - Give you a separate schedule of the amounts for those services before you take up the room.
  - Give you an itemised account of your individual use if you use the services.
- **Homes Victoria and registered housing agencies (s 109A):**
  - They may impose a service charge for "laundry… services or facilities" in a rooming house declared under s 19(2) or (3). This applies only if it isn't possible or practicable to accurately measure your use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - The charge can't exceed the cost of providing the service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - They must give you written notice of the charge or any change to it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - You can apply to the Tribunal to have the charge withdrawn or varied [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - The retrieved text doesn't say whether a coin meter counts as "accurately measuring" use. Nothing in these sections covers a private operator's laundry fee.
- **Laundry standard:** The Rooming House Standards Regulations require a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents, plus a wash trough or basin and a clothes line. They don't mention charging [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). The version I found is dated 1 December 2024, so I can't confirm it is current for October 2026.

## What you can do

1. **Ask for the schedule of service charges and itemised account.** If the operator charges for services, s 109 requires the schedule before you took up the room [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check who your operator is.** If it's Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, you can ask for written notice of the charge and its cost basis. You can also apply to the Tribunal to withdraw or vary it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Challenge the charge as a house rule, if it comes from one.** An operator may make house rules about using facilities [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). They must be reasonable and enforced fairly [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A resident may apply to the Tribunal to declare a house rule unreasonable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). These sections come from the earlier version dated 25 November 2025 (v111). The v115 excerpt I retrieved cuts off before them, so check the current wording.
4. **Check the standard.** Ask whether the house meets the one-machine-per-12-residents laundry standard [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

For a definite answer on your situation, the Tribunal or Consumer Affairs Victoria's Director of Consumer Affairs would be the next step. The documents I retrieved don't cover them in this context.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. The answer says the standard requires 'a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents'. It says the documents 'don't say whether a rooming house operator may charge' and the standard does 'not mention charging', which counts as the law not requiring the machines to be free. It states the s 109 requirement to give 'a separate schedule of the amounts for those services before you take up the room'. Its next step is 'Ask for the schedule of service charges', which it ties to the schedule being required before moving in.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three are asserted: the answer never says the machines must be free, it says 'The Act does regulate how service charges are handled' rather than that there are no rules, and it limits the cost cap to 'Homes Victoria and registered housing agencies (s 109A)', adding that 'Nothing in these sections covers a private operator's laundry fee.'

version-cited.reason: No: the answer names the in-force versions ('rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf' / 97-109aa115 for the Act and 23-10sra002 dated 1 December 2024 for the Standards Regulations), but step 3 tells the user to challenge the charge as a house rule using sections from 'the earlier version dated 25 November 2025 (v111)' (97-109aa111). That presents a superseded version's rule as a step the user can take, which counts as relying on it despite the caveat, and deleting it would remove a substantive step from the answer.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
## What the law says (as at 1 October 2025)

**Advertising**
- The Act version in force on 1 October 2025 in the retrieved documents is *rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf* (Residential Tenancies Act 1997, dated 6 August 2025, version 110 going by the file title). It has no rule on advertising premises that fail the minimum standards. Section 65A is there, followed directly by s 66 [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- A ban on advertising such premises, s 65B, appears only in later versions: *rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf* (25 November 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf* (13 October 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Those versions say a provider or agent must not advertise or offer premises to let unless they reasonably believe the premises comply with the rental minimum standards. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The documents don't say when s 65B started. So I can't say it applied on 1 October 2025, and I can't confirm the ad was unlawful on that date. The documents show that s 65B was inserted by Act No. 6/2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), but not its commencement date.

**The minimum standard on mould**
- In the Regulations version in force on that date, *rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf* (1 July 2025), Schedule 4 clause 8 says: "Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure." [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- The later version, *rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf*, has the same wording [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- The v004 reprint doesn't state its own version number in the text I retrieved. "v004" comes from the file title.

**Duty on the provider**
- Under s 65A(1) of v110, the provider must make sure the premises meet the prescribed minimum standards on or before the day the renter moves in. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## Is the photo enough to prove non-compliance?

Not on its own, going by the documents.
- The standard covers mould and damp "caused by or related to the building structure" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). A photo can show mould, but it doesn't show what caused it.
- The documents don't say what evidence is needed to prove a breach, so I can't say more than that.

## What the renter can do or ask

- **After moving in:** if the premises don't meet the minimum standards on or immediately after the day the renter enters into occupation, the renter may issue a request for urgent repairs to bring them up to standard (s 65A(2), v110) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Maintenance:** the provider must also keep the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation (s 68(1), v110) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Before signing:** the renter can ask the agent whether the room meets the mould and damp standard and what caused the mould. Regulation 16(2) lists information a provider must disclose to rental applicants, including whether the premises comply with the minimum standards. It also covers any repair notice about mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure in the last 3 years [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). I only retrieved that regulation in the later v005 version [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) and the 2022 v002 version [[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). I didn't retrieve the v004 text, so I can't confirm the wording in force on 1 October 2025.

The documents don't say how to complain about an ad or where to take a dispute about one. They also don't say what enforcement steps are available. I haven't filled those gaps from outside knowledge.

must-mention.reason: Yes. question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
## What the law says

I've used the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", dated 13 October 2026. The file name gives it as version 115, and it is the latest version retrieved. I'm treating it as the version in force on 15 October 2026. The text I quote also appears in the earlier versions I retrieved, v110 (6 Aug 2025) and v111 (25 Nov 2025), but I rely only on v115.

- **Consent is required.** A renter must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the rented premises without the rental provider's written consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **No consent means the arrangement is invalid.** An assignment or sub-letting without the rental provider's consent is invalid unless the Tribunal has determined that consent is not required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **You are exposed to a notice to vacate.** A rental provider may give the renter a notice to vacate if the renter has assigned or sub-let, or purported to assign or sub-let, any part of the premises without consent. The notice must give a termination date at least 14 days after it is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

So the risk in this situation is to you, as the renter. If the agent finds out, the law lets them give you a 14-day notice to vacate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

- **Tell the agent and ask for written consent.** If you want to regularise things rather than remove your friend, the rental provider must not unreasonably withhold consent, and cannot refuse on the basis of an attribute in section 6 of the *Equal Opportunity Act 2010* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). They also cannot demand or receive a fee for giving consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Apply to the Tribunal if consent is refused.** If the rental provider withholds consent and you believe that is unreasonable, you can apply for a determination that consent isn't required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Removing your friend.** The documents I retrieved don't say how a renter ends a friend's stay or makes them leave. They also don't say whether letting a friend stay counts as "sub-letting" under section 81, for example if no rent is paid. The provisions I found deal with consent to sub-letting and the rental provider's right to give a notice to vacate. I can't say from these documents what steps you must take, so I won't guess. For that, you could seek advice from the community legal organisations or Consumer Affairs Victoria, as the notice-to-vacate form suggests [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

On written consent, the answer says 'A renter must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the rented premises without the rental provider's written consent.' The harder point, that the answer depends on the arrangement and names a deciding fact, is covered by 'They also don't say whether letting a friend stay counts as "sub-letting" under section 81, for example if no rent is paid.' question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I retrieved don't contain the Victorian law for an ordinary month-to-month tenancy as it stood on 1 November 2019. I can't confirm the retaliation rules that apply to you.

## Which version applies
- On 1 November 2019 the version in force was the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* file **rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf**, dated 2 July 2019 (version 088, going by the file name) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- The next version, **rta-1997-v089-2019-12-04.pdf**, is dated 4 December 2019. That is after your date, so it wasn't in force then [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf).
- Later versions use "renter" and "residential rental provider" wording and have the repairs sections (ss 72–77). These are v101 dated 7 September 2022 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf), v110 dated 6 August 2025 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) and v111 dated 25 November 2025 [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* "Form 6" says you can challenge a notice if you think it was given "because you tried to exercise your rights as a renter" [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). That form is from the 2021 regulations (the copies I found are dated 2022–2026), so it doesn't apply to a notice given in 2019 [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says (2019 version retrieved)
The v088 text I retrieved covers only **rooming houses**, not ordinary tenancies. It does not include the ordinary-tenancy notice and retaliation sections.

If you live in a rooming house, v088 says:
- A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the prescribed form, addressed to you, and signed. It must also give the reason for the notice and a termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- A notice under s 142ZA (end of a fixed term) is "of no effect" if it was given in response to you exercising, or proposing to exercise, a right under the Act. The same applies if it was given in response to a report you made under s 116(2) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- A notice for threats and intimidation (s 142ZD) is also "of no effect" if it was given in response to you exercising a right under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- You can't challenge a s 142ZA notice at the Tribunal after 14 days from the day it was given. For s 142ZJ or 142ZK notices the limit is 30 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

Section 142ZA applies to fixed-term agreements, so the retrieved text doesn't show a retaliation rule for a month-to-month rooming house resident, except for s 142ZD threat notices.

## What you can check and ask
1. **Type of tenancy.** Confirm whether you are in a rooming house or an ordinary rental. Only the rooming-house rules were retrieved [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Form and content of the notice.** Check that it is in the prescribed form, is addressed and signed, gives a reason, and states a termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
3. **The stated reason.** See which section the notice relies on. If it is s 142ZD (threats), the "no effect if in response to exercising a right" rule applies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Timing.** Note the date it was given. The same-day timing after your repair follow-up is useful evidence, but the documents don't say how the Tribunal treats it.
5. **Deadlines.** Act quickly. The only deadlines I found are the 14 and 30 days above, and they are for rooming-house notices [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
6. **Repairs rights.** The 2019 repairs provisions weren't retrieved. The repairs sections I found (reporting damage, urgent repairs, non-urgent repairs) are from 2022 and later versions and may differ from the 2019 law [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

I tried a follow-up search for the ordinary-tenancy notice and Tribunal challenge provisions, but it failed. I'd suggest getting advice from a tenancy advice service or community legal centre, since I can't confirm the 2019 rules for your tenancy.

It also does not mention the 60-day window to challenge at VCAT, citing only 14-day and 30-day rooming-house limits.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
# Rental bidding and your withdrawn application (as at 1 October 2025)

**Version used:** the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", dated 6 August 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Its file name indicates version 110. The excerpt doesn't print an "Authorised Version No." line, so I'm relying on the file name. It is the latest retrieved version dated on or before 1 October 2025. I can't confirm from the documents that no other version sat between it and your date.

## What the law says

- **Fixed advertised rent.** A rental provider or agent must not advertise or offer premises unless the rent is advertised or offered as a fixed amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **No inviting higher offers.** They must not "solicit or otherwise invite an offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount" (s 30F(3)). The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Accepting unsolicited higher offers.** Version 110 contains no provision on this. Only the later versions have a s 30F(4), which bars accepting an unsolicited or uninvited higher offer. Those are dated 25 November 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and 13 October 2026 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), so they post-date your 1 October 2025 question. Whether a rule against accepting unsolicited higher offers applied to you on that date is not answered by the version I've treated as in force. Nothing in the retrieved documents shows when s 30F(4) started.
- **False or misleading rent advertising.** A provider or agent who promotes or advertises premises must not make a false or misleading representation about the rent (s 30G). The penalty is the same 60 or 300 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Misleading conduct.** Providers and agents must not induce someone to enter an agreement by misleading or deceptive conduct, including false representations about the rent payable (s 30E) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**Not covered:** The documents don't address an agent wrongly recording an applicant as having "withdrawn". They also don't set out any right to be told why an application failed, or any rule against relisting at a higher rent as such. I can't say that conduct is unlawful from these documents alone.

## What you can do

- **Ask what happened.** Your facts could fit s 30F(3) if the agent invited higher offers. They could fit s 30G or s 30E if the advertised rent was misleading. They would not fit s 30F(3) if the higher offer was unsolicited, because version 110 has no provision on accepting those.
- **Seek a Tribunal order.** The Act notes that s 472(1A) allows Tribunal orders on a contravention of s 30E [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The excerpt doesn't say what those orders are, and I found no equivalent compensation provision for rent-related breaches.
- **Compensation for discrimination.** Section 210AA allows a compensation application for loss from discrimination under the Division [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). It applies only if you think the withdrawal was really a refusal based on a protected attribute (s 30A).

## What to save as evidence

The documents contain no evidence checklist, so this is general practical advice. I'd keep:

- The original advertisement, with the advertised rent and its date, and screenshots of the new, higher listing.
- Your application and any confirmation.
- The "withdrawn" email, with full headers, and all other messages with the agent.
- Any message that invites, mentions or confirms higher offers.
- Notes of calls or inspections, with dates and names.

must-mention.reason: Yes (pass). All four points are covered. (1) Relisting is covered by "[the documents don't] set out ... any rule against relisting at a higher rent as such. I can't say that conduct is unlawful from these documents alone." (2) Inviting higher offers is banned under s 30F(3). (3) The hardest point, unsolicited offers, is covered by "Version 110 contains no provision on this. Only the later versions have a s 30F(4) ... so they post-date your 1 October 2025 question" and "They would not fit s 30F(3) if the higher offer was unsolicited, because version 110 has no provision on accepting those." Despite some hedging about versions, a reader can tell that accepting an unsolicited offer was not banned on that date. (4) The false 'withdrawn' email is covered by "The documents don't address an agent wrongly recording an applicant as having 'withdrawn'."

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer makes none of the three claims: it says the documents don't set out 'any rule against relisting at a higher rent as such. I can't say that conduct is unlawful', that 'Version 110 contains no provision on this' for unsolicited higher offers (the s 30F(4) versions 'post-date your 1 October 2025 question'), and it never says the applicant can force the agent to rent to them.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "version 110", dated 6 August 2025 (file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf" and link 97-109aa110), and applies ss 30F(3) and 30G from that version. It mentions the later versions 111 and 115 only to say their s 30F(4) post-dates 1 October 2025, and never presents that rule as law or as a step the user can take.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
## What the law says

I've used the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version No. 115**, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf"). It is the version in force on 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

- **Refusal must be reasonable.** A residential rental provider (the owner) "must not unreasonably refuse to consent" to a renter keeping a pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A flat "no" from the agent doesn't settle the matter.
- **There is a 14-day deadline.** The provider is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days after being given the request, they apply to the Tribunal [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Only the Tribunal can decide that a refusal is reasonable. The provider can apply for an order that it is reasonable to refuse consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The Tribunal's test.** It can order that you may keep the pet. It can also order that refusal is reasonable, but only if it is satisfied of that [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It may consider the following [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):
  - the type of pet
  - the character and nature of the premises
  - the appliances, fixtures and fittings
  - whether refusal is permitted under any Act
  - any prescribed matters
  - any other matter it considers relevant
- **Allergy.** The Act doesn't list an owner's allergy as a ground, and it doesn't say how the owner rarely visiting would be treated. An allergy could only come in under "any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say how the Tribunal would weigh it, so I can't tell you how it would come out.

## Applying this to you

You sent the request three weeks ago, which is more than 14 days. If the owner (or agent) did not apply to the Tribunal within those 14 days, the Act treats the owner as having consented [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I can't tell from the documents whether anyone applied.

## What you can do

1. **Check whether a Tribunal application was made** within 14 days of the owner receiving your request. If none was, you can rely on the deemed consent under s 71C(2) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Confirm your request was valid.** It must be on the form approved by the Director and given to the residential rental provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You sent it to the agent, and the retrieved text doesn't say whether that counts as giving it to the provider. Keep proof of when and how you sent it.
3. **Put it in writing.** Tell the agent that the owner must not unreasonably refuse, and that without a Tribunal application within 14 days consent is deemed given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Ask for written consent.** Under s 71A you may keep a pet if the provider consents in writing or the Tribunal orders it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Act also says deemed consent applies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), but written consent avoids disputes.

**Not covered:** The retrieved text doesn't cover what happens if you keep the dog while the owner disputes deemed consent. The table of contents lists a section on notice to vacate when a pet is kept without consent (s 91ZZG), but I didn't retrieve its text [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Check it before you act. Consider getting advice from a tenancy advocacy service or Consumer Affairs Victoria as well.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the answer states that the provider 'is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days after being given the request, they apply to the Tribunal'; it applies this to the three-week timeline ('If the owner (or agent) did not apply to the Tribunal within those 14 days, the Act treats the owner as having consented'); and it gives a next step, 'Check whether a Tribunal application was made within 14 days', along with putting it to the agent in writing.

The answer asserts none of the failure conditions: it says "A flat 'no' from the agent doesn't settle the matter," places the onus on the provider to "apply to the Tribunal" within 14 days rather than requiring the renter to apply, and says of the allergy that "I can't tell you how it would come out."

The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, **Authorised Version No. 115**, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026' (file 'rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf', link 97-109aa115), which is the version in force on 15 October 2026, and every rule it applies (ss 71A, 71C and the Tribunal factors) is cited to that version only, with no reliance on any other version.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Version applied:** On 1 October 2025 the version in force was *rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf* (Residential Tenancies Act 1997, dated 6 August 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The file name shows version 110, but the retrieved text doesn't print an "Authorised Version No." line, so I'm relying on the file name for that. Later versions, v111 (25 November 2025) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and v115 (13 October 2026) [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), were not in force on that date. They also change the sale notice period from 60 to 90 days, so don't use them for a notice given now.

## What the law says

- **The notice stays in force until it is formally withdrawn.** A notice to vacate is withdrawn only if a written notice of withdrawal is given. It must be signed by the person who gave the notice (the landlord) and by the person it was given to (you) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The buyer pulling out does not withdraw it, and the landlord not withdrawing it doesn't either.
- **A sale notice can still be valid without that buyer.** A landlord may give a notice if the premises are, immediately after the termination date, "to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession". The notice must give at least 60 days' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The wording covers being offered for sale, not only a completed contract. My reading is that the landlord could still rely on the notice if they relist the property. The documents don't deal with this exact situation.
- **You don't have to leave just because of the notice.** The landlord must apply to the Tribunal for a possession order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can't decide that application before the termination date in the notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The application can be made any time after the notice is given, up to 30 days after the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **When the Tribunal must make the order.** It must make one if it is satisfied that:
  - the landlord was entitled to give the notice;
  - the notice has not been withdrawn;
  - you are still in the premises after the termination date; and
  - making the order is "reasonable and proportionate" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **What counts as reasonable and proportionate.** The Tribunal looks at factors including whether another course of action is reasonably available instead of an order, and the landlord's behaviour [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the landlord for a signed written withdrawal.** It only works if both you and the landlord sign it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say the landlord must agree.
2. **Challenge the notice's validity at the Tribunal.** You can apply on or before the hearing of the possession application. The application must be made within 30 days after the notice was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If that period has already passed, the documents don't say whether you can still apply.
3. **Check the notice itself.** It is not valid unless it:
   - is in the prescribed form, addressed to you and signed;
   - states the reason for giving it;
   - is accompanied by supporting documentary evidence; and
   - specifies the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
4. **Check the timing.** The notice must allow at least 60 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Where it relies on a contract of sale, it must be given within 14 days after the contract was entered into or its last condition was satisfied [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
5. **Raise the buyer's withdrawal at any hearing.** It is relevant to whether the landlord still intends to sell, and to whether an order is reasonable and proportionate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
6. **Know the re-letting rule.** If the landlord gets possession under a sale notice, they must not re-let the premises as a residence within 6 months after the notice was given. The penalty is 150 penalty units for an individual [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This doesn't apply if the Tribunal determines the premises may be let [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't say whether you'd have to leave by the termination date if no application has been made. For advice on your own notice, speak to a tenancy advice service or legal help.

The hardest one, that the answer depends on the notice's ground and evidence, is covered by the wording "to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession" and "covers being offered for sale, not only a completed contract". This is backed by the checks that the notice "states the reason" and "is accompanied by supporting documentary evidence", and the separate rule "where it relies on a contract of sale". The answer also states the 60-day minimum and that withdrawal must be in writing and signed by both landlord and renter. It gives both next steps: ask for a signed withdrawal, or challenge the notice at the Tribunal within 30 days.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
## What the law says

I've applied the versions in force on 1 October 2025. These are the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", dated 6 August 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (file "rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf", dated 1 July 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The version number "v110" comes from the file name. The text I retrieved doesn't print an "Authorised Version No." itself.

- **Notice is required.** A rental provider must give the renter at least 60 days notice, in the prescribed form, of a proposed rent increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **The notice must contain set details.** It must state the amount of the increase, the method used to calculate it, and your right to ask the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate within 30 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). It may only provide for one increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **The prescribed form is Form 5.** It says "A valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases." [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- **An invalid increase has no effect.** "A rent increase in contravention of this section is invalid." [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- **Other limits.** Rent can't be increased at intervals of less than 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). In a fixed-term agreement, rent can't go up before the term ends unless the agreement provides for it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## Do you have to pay, and from when?

On what you've described, **no, you don't have to pay the higher rent yet.** An email from the agent isn't the prescribed-form notice, and an increase without a valid notice is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). I'm assuming the email didn't meet the Form 5 requirements. If it did include everything Form 5 requires, that would change the answer.

The documents don't give a start date for an increase that hasn't been properly notified. A valid increase can only take effect once at least 60 days' notice has been given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If a proper Form 5 notice were given to you today (1 October 2025), the earliest start would be 60 days later, which is around 30 November 2025.

The later version of the Regulations (v005, dated 25 November 2025) changes Form 5 to 90 days [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). That version was not in force on 1 October 2025. It could matter if the notice is only given after it takes effect, but I can't confirm that from these documents.

## What you can do

- **Ask for a proper notice.** Ask the agent in writing for a valid Form 5 notice. It must show the new rent, the start date and the calculation method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Check the 12-month rule and your agreement.** See whether the last increase was less than 12 months ago, and whether you're in a fixed term [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Challenge a proper notice if you get one.** You can apply in writing to the Director to investigate within 30 days of the notice being given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). After that you can apply to VCAT to have the proposed rent declared excessive [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). If you apply to VCAT, you must pay the increased rent from the date on the notice unless VCAT decides otherwise [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**Not covered:** The documents don't say whether you can agree informally to an emailed increase. They also don't say whether you can recover rent you've already paid at the higher rate.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered: Form 5 is identified as the prescribed form, at least 60 days' notice is stated, and the answer says the email isn't a valid notice ('no, you don't have to pay the higher rent yet. An email from the agent isn't the prescribed-form notice, and an increase without a valid notice is invalid'). It also gives next steps, such as asking the agent in writing for a proper notice and applying to the Director to investigate within 30 days of a proper notice.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says "no, you don't have to pay the higher rent yet" and gives a 60-day minimum ("the earliest start would be 60 days later, which is around 30 November 2025"). It mentions 90 days only for v005, which it says "was not in force on 1 October 2025". It never ties the start date to the email, and it does not rule out email notices, since it says "If it did include everything Form 5 requires, that would change the answer."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions: the Act as "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", dated 6 August 2025 (link 97-109aa110), and the Regulations as "rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf", dated 1 July 2025 (link 21-3sra004). It applies only rules from those versions, including the 60-day notice and earliest start of 30 November 2025. It mentions the later Regulations v005 (90 days) only to say that version was not in force on 1 October 2025 and the law changes later. Deleting that mention would not change the substance of the answer.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
## What the law says

The version in force on 15 October 2026 is **rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf** (Residential Tenancies Act 1997, dated 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Its title shows version "v115". The documents don't show an "Authorised Version" label beyond that file name.

- **Don't damage the premises.** A renter must not intentionally or negligently damage the rented premises. Fair wear and tear isn't counted as damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether dog chewing is damage or wear and tear.
- **You must tell the owner in writing.** A renter who becomes aware of damage must give written notice "as soon as practicable". The notice must say that the damage happened and what it is. Email is allowed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Section 72AA also requires written notice of damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). So you can't quietly deal with it and say nothing.
- **Leave the property in the same condition.** At the end of the agreement, the renter must leave the premises as far as practicable in the same condition as when they moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Pets need consent.** A renter may keep a pet only with the rental provider's written consent or a Tribunal order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The owner decides how the repair is handled.** If the damage was caused by the renter's failure to take care, the owner may give a written repair notice. It can either:
  - require the renter to repair it at their own expense within 14 days, or
  - say the owner will do the repair and the renter is liable for the reasonable cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **If the owner does the repair,** the renter is liable for the reasonable cost once the owner gives the cost particulars in writing. The renter must reimburse within 14 days after the repairs are completed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Hardship provisions can extend this by 14 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **If the owner asks you to repair it,** the work must be done "in a proper and tradesman-like manner" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Only qualified people should do repairs.** The standard-form agreement summary in the earlier regulations, **rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf** (25 November 2025), says "Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs—both urgent and non-urgent" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The part of the current regulations I retrieved, **rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf** (30 June 2026), doesn't show that clause [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm it from the current version.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Notify the owner or agent in writing now.** Describe the skirting board damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Offer to repair it, and ask whether they'll accept that.** The Act lets the owner choose between you repairing it and them repairing it at your cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you use a tradesperson, use a suitably qualified one [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). A quick fix without telling the owner doesn't remove the duty to give written notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Document the condition.** Take dated photos. At the end of the agreement, the owner or agent must complete the final inspection within 10 days and give you a chance to attend. They must allow for fair wear and tear [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **If you can't pay within 14 days,** you can ask the Tribunal for an extension. Alternatively, you can give written notice of hardship for an extra 14 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Would it affect the owner's insurance?

**The retrieved documents don't say.** They contain nothing about the owner's insurance or how damage or repairs might affect a policy. I can't answer that part from these sources. The owner or their insurer would be the one to ask.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. (1) Written notice: the renter must give written notice of damage "as soon as practicable". (2) Responsibility and condition: the renter must not damage the premises, is liable for repair or its reasonable cost, and must leave the premises in the same condition allowing for fair wear and tear. This point is weakened by the line "The documents don't say whether dog chewing is damage or wear and tear," but the rest of the answer clearly treats the chewing as damage the renter must notify and pay for. (3) Insurance: the answer says the documents "contain nothing about the owner's insurance". (4) Next steps: notify the owner in writing and offer to repair.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the failure conditions are asserted. The answer rejects a quiet repair ("So you can't quietly deal with it and say nothing"), states no insurance outcome as fact ("The retrieved documents don't say. They contain nothing about the owner's insurance"), and never says the renter must pay the owner's insurance excess.

version-cited.reason: No: the answer names 'rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf' and the Act v115 ('97-109aa115'), but its step 2 advice to 'use a suitably qualified one [4]' is sourced from the non-in-force 'rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf' (21-3sra005), which counts as relying on an earlier version even though it adds a caveat.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** The version of the Regulations in force on 1 March 2023 doesn't set a minimum number of circuits for a rental. The documents don't say whether an overloaded circuit is a repair issue.

The version I relied on is *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf", dated 1 June 2022 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The file name shows it as version 002, but the excerpt I retrieved doesn't print an Authorised Version number. The later versions (1 July 2025, 25 November 2025 and 30 June 2026) post-date your question, so I haven't relied on them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Electrical safety standard (Schedule 4, clause 9).** All power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to a switchboard-type circuit breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000. They must also be connected to a switchboard-type residual current device (RCD) meeting one of the listed standards [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **This standard wasn't yet in force on 1 March 2023.** Clause 9 applies "on and from 29 March 2023" [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Nothing on circuit numbers.** Clause 9 says nothing about how many circuits a rental needs or how power points must be split between them [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Overload tripping isn't addressed.** The retrieved text doesn't say whether a breaker tripping under load is a breach.
- **Rental provider's general duties.** Under the standard rental agreement terms, the rental provider must:
  - make sure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards;
  - keep them in good repair and fit for occupation; and
  - do the safety-related activities in Part C of the agreement [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## What you can ask for

1. **An electrical safety check.** The rental provider must have all electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provide checked every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician. On your request, they must give you the date of the most recent check in writing [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **A check if none was done recently.** If no check was done in the 2 years before you moved in, the rental provider must arrange one as soon as practicable [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). You could ask for this and raise the tripping with the electrician.
3. **A repair, if the circuit or wiring is faulty.** Notify the rental provider in writing as soon as practicable. They must carry out non-urgent repairs in a reasonable time. If the repair isn't done within 14 days of your notice, you can apply to VCAT for an order [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
4. **An urgent repair, in limited cases.** The documents say urgent repairs include failure of an essential service or appliance for hot water, cooking, heating or laundering that the rental provider supplies. Section 3(1) of the Act has the full definition, and it isn't in the documents I retrieved [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Whether a tripping breaker counts is not covered.

## Limits of the documents

The documents don't say whether adding circuits or upgrading the switchboard is something you can require. They also don't say how a VCAT decision would treat an overloaded circuit. An electrician's report would help your request.

must-mention.reason: Both points are covered. The output says the version in force 'doesn't set a minimum number of circuits for a rental' and that clause 9 'says nothing about how many circuits a rental needs'. On next steps, the hardest point, it says the rental provider 'must give you the date of the most recent check in writing' on request, and it also covers requesting a repair, with urgent repair noted for limited cases.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer states that the Regulations "doesn't set a minimum number of circuits for a rental" and that the circuit breaker and RCD standard "wasn't yet in force on 1 March 2023" because it "applies 'on and from 29 March 2023'", so it asserts neither a minimum circuit number nor that the standard already applied.

version-cited.reason: No. The answer names the Regulations' version (file "rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf", link 21-3sra002, dated 1 June 2022), but it mentions the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 only as "Section 3(1) of the Act" and never gives Authorised Version No. 101 or any other version, so a required document is named without a version.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I retrieved don't say outright whether a rooming house operator can charge for coin-operated washing machines. They do set rules on charging for services, and those rules give you some things to ask for.

## What the law says

I've used *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", dated 13 October 2026. This is the version in force on 15 October 2026. The file name indicates version 115, but the extract I saw doesn't show the "Authorised Version No." wording itself.

- **Charges outside rent are limited.** An operator may charge separately for electricity, gas and water only if the room is separately metered and the operator pays those bills. The charge can't be more than the supplier's charge [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That section is about consumption in the room, so it doesn't clearly cover a shared laundry.
- **Charges for services come with disclosure duties.** If an operator charges for services, it must give you a separate schedule of the amounts before you take up the room. If you use those services, it must give you an itemised account of your own use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Homes Victoria and registered housing agencies have special rules.**
  - They may impose a service charge for "laundry… services or facilities", but only if it isn't possible or practicable to accurately measure your use.
  - The charge must not exceed the cost of providing the service.
  - They must give you written notice of the charge and of any change to it.
  - You can apply to the Tribunal to have the charge withdrawn or varied [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - This applies only to rooming houses declared under s 19(2) or (3) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). My reading, which the Act doesn't state, is that a coin-operated machine does measure use, so this provision may not fit it.
- **Laundry standards don't mention fees.** The Rooming House Standards Regulations 2023, in the copy I found (dated 1 December 2024), require a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents, from 26 February 2024. They also require a wash trough or basin and a clothes line or drying facility [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). They say nothing about whether the machines can be coin-operated. I haven't seen a 2026 version of these regulations, so I can't confirm this is still current.

**Not covered:** I found no provision in the retrieved documents that expressly allows or bans coin-operated laundry fees in a private rooming house.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask for the schedule of service charges and itemised accounts.** The operator must give you these if it charges for services [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check who runs the house.** If it's Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, you can ask for written notice of the charge and ask the Tribunal to withdraw or vary it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Check the number of machines.** Two machines should meet the standard unless the house has more than 24 residents. That follows from the one-per-12 requirement [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). A broken machine is a repair issue.
4. **Look at the house rules.**
   - The retrieved text of the current version doesn't include the house-rules sections.
   - An earlier version, from 25 November 2025, says operators may make house rules about using facilities. The rules must be reasonable and applied fairly. A resident can apply to the Tribunal to have a rule declared unreasonable [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
   - I haven't confirmed these sections are unchanged in the 13 October 2026 version, so check the current Act.

I can't tell you from these documents whether your operator's charge is lawful. A tenancy advice service or the Director of Consumer Affairs could confirm that for your house.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered: the one-per-12 washing machine standard; the law not requiring free machines ('They say nothing about whether the machines can be coin-operated' and 'no provision... that expressly allows or bans coin-operated laundry fees'); the schedule of charges ('a separate schedule of the amounts before you take up the room'); and the next step ('Ask for the schedule of service charges and itemised accounts').

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three failing claims is made. The answer never says the machines must be free. It does not say there are no rules on charges, and instead states the operator 'must give you a separate schedule of the amounts' and 'an itemised account'. It also limits the cost cap to Homes Victoria and registered housing agencies, stating 'This applies only to rooming houses declared under s 19(2) or (3)', rather than applying it to all rooming houses.
