question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Short answer:** The Act version in force on 1 October 2025 has no rule on advertising. A photo of mould is also not enough on its own to prove the place breaches the minimum standards.

## What the law says

**1. Advertising**
- On 1 October 2025 the Act in force was *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf" (6 August 2025, labelled v110). In that version, s 65A on rental minimum standards is followed directly by s 66. There is no advertising provision [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- A rule on advertising, s 65B, appears only in later versions. These are "rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf" (25 November 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf" (13 October 2026) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Under s 65B, a provider or agent must not advertise premises unless they reasonably believe the premises comply with the rental minimum standards. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The documents don't say when s 65B commenced. So I can't say whether it applied on 1 October 2025, and I haven't assumed it did. The only version I can attribute to that date (v110) doesn't contain it.
- Even under s 65B, the test is the provider's reasonable belief that the premises comply. A photo of apparent mould in an ad might suggest the provider didn't hold that belief, but the documents don't say so.

**2. Is the photo enough to prove a breach?**
- The relevant standard is in the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, "rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf" (1 July 2025), Schedule 4, clause 8. It says each room "must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- So the standard covers mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure. A photo shows that mould appears to be present. It doesn't show the cause. The retrieved documents say nothing about what evidence is needed to prove a breach, so I can't say more on that.

## What a renter can do or ask

- **Ask for disclosure.** Under reg 16(2) of the same regulations, the provider must disclose to a rental applicant whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards. They must also disclose whether they have received a repair notice about mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure in the last 3 years [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). These are prescribed for s 30D(e) of the Act. The Act's text of s 30D wasn't in the retrieved material.
- **Rely on the provider's duty before moving in.** Under s 65A(1), the provider must ensure the premises meet the prescribed minimum standards on or before the day the renter enters occupation. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Request urgent repairs after moving in.** If the premises don't comply on or immediately after the day the renter enters occupation, the renter may issue a request for urgent repairs to bring them up to the standards (s 65A(2)) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Rely on the general repair duty.** Under s 68, the provider must provide and maintain the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**Not covered:** The documents don't say when s 65B commenced, how a breach of it is enforced, or what evidence proves a mould breach.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: it states the mould and damp standard ('must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure'), it says the photo alone doesn't prove a breach ('A photo of mould is also not enough on its own to prove the place breaches the minimum standards'), and it gives next steps such as asking for disclosure and requesting urgent repairs after moving in (s 65A(2)).

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer does not say either prohibited thing: it states "A photo of mould is also not enough on its own to prove the place breaches the minimum standards" and "The Act version in force on 1 October 2025 has no rule on advertising," attributing s 65B only to later versions without asserting it applied on that date.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
**Version applied:** On 15 October 2026 the version in force was the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf" (version 115 by file name, dated 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I also checked the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf" (version 009 by file name, dated 30 June 2026) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **You need written consent to let someone else have part of the rental.** A renter must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the rented premises without the rental provider's written consent (s 81(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The regulations' standard terms say the same [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Without consent, the arrangement is invalid.** An assignment or sub-letting without consent is invalid unless the Tribunal has determined that consent is not required (s 81(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Your own tenancy is at risk.** If a renter has assigned or sub-let, or purported to, any part of the premises without consent, the rental provider may give the renter a notice to vacate (s 91ZV). The termination date must be at least 14 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The standard terms also say the rental provider may give notice to vacate in this case [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The agent can enter to check.** Entry is allowed if the provider or agent has reasonable grounds to believe the renter has failed to comply with their duties under the Act or the agreement (s 86(1)(e)). This needs at least 24 hours' written notice (s 85(b)(iii)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

- **Tell the agent.** The documents do not require you to report the friend, but the risk above comes from the lack of consent. Raising it yourself is the safest way to deal with that risk. This is my practical suggestion, not something the documents say.
- **Ask your friend to leave.** The documents do not say whether a friend staying with you counts as "sub-letting". That probably turns on the facts, such as whether they pay you. The documents don't address this.
- **Seek consent only if you want them to stay.** The provider must not unreasonably withhold consent (s 81(2)). If it is withheld, you can ask the Tribunal to decide that consent isn't needed (s 82) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This doesn't help if you want the friend gone.

## What the documents don't cover

The retrieved documents give no step-by-step process for a renter to remove a friend or other occupant who refuses to leave. The notice to vacate in Form 6 is for rental providers to give renters [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I can't tell you from these documents how to force a friend out. For that, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria (consumer.vic.gov.au/renting) or a community legal centre.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. The output says sub-letting needs the rental provider's written consent (s 81(1)). The hardest point, that the answer depends on the arrangement, is covered by 'whether a friend staying with you counts as "sub-letting"... probably turns on the facts, such as whether they pay you', which names payment as a deciding fact.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer gives no fixed process for removing the friend, no lock-out, no claim that the friend has no rights, and no claim that the friend can apply to VCAT to join the lease; it says "I can't tell you from these documents how to force a friend out," and its 14-day notice (s 91ZV) and Tribunal application (s 82) concern the rental provider and the renter, not the friend.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf (version 115 by file name, dated 13 October 2026)" with link 97-109aa115, and the only other document it relies on is the in-force Regulations "version 009" dated 30 June 2026, so it applies no out-of-force version.
